Moving Our Intelligence Outside of the Constraints of Biology Something remarkable has begun to happen. We are not just studying intelligence. We are building it. As you will come to see, many of the key principles that allowed our biological intelligence to emerge—prediction, feedback, reinforcement, memory updating—are foundational to how modern artificial intelligence systems operate. Miracles of Efficiency As we build AI and discover the intense energy consumption that it requires, the more impressive our per-watt of energy biological intelligence seems. And in some ways, AI is a very clever solution for biological intelligence, for us , to escape the limitation of energy. To plug intelligence into the power grid. And from this perspective, we will explore how we can plug back into AI to benefit directly from that. The miraculous efficiency of our brains isn’t just impressive—it’s an evolutionary necessity. Energy has always been a type of rate-limiting factor for biological intelligence. In the biological world, brains evolved not to be perfect but to make hyperefficient use of a very small amount of available energy. Recognizing this can perhaps help us feel more grounded and less threatened by the accelerating AI revolution. In the pages ahead, we will explore what happens when we take something profound that was developed under extreme energy constraints (biological intelligence) and create a version of intelligence that we can plug into massive energy resources. Desirable Difficulty and the Emergence of Consciousness But before we seek to understand what AI might become, we need to fully grasp what we already are: the conscious intelligence that slowly and magnificently evolved over millions of years under extraordinary constraint, from which artificial intelligence is now rapidly emerging. We will explore how emotional processing, which began in our brains as a survival alert system, was central to the emergence of our own consciousness. We will explore how consciousness arises within the relationship between the brain and the body. And how the introduction of constraints to AI of entering the physical world through robotics may be the key to the emergence of some form of conscious self-awareness in artificial intelligence as well. This isn’t just a technical argument. It is a philosophical one. It invites us to consider intelligence as a kind of elegant emergence—shaped in part by the scarcity of fuel, the delicacy of evolution, the trade-offs of biology. How consciousness itself is a by-product of desirable difficulty. The idea of desirable difficulty is explored in Malcolm Gladwell’s amazing book David and Goliath . 14 At the heart of that book lies the work of Dr. Robert Bjork, who coined the term and pioneered the concept as a foundation of human learning. 15 Gladwell’s book explores how what we often perceive as disadvantages—such as poverty, learning disabilities, or underdog status—can actually create conditions for extraordinary advantage. He argues that real strength can emerge from constraint, adversity, and limitation. 16 The shepherd boy David was not a weaker opponent to the armored Goliath—he was a new kind of opponent, using speed, ingenuity, and asymmetric strategy. Our conversation here echoes this idea that the struggle itself—the “desirable difficulty”—is not a barrier to greatness, but often the very path to it. Through stories ranging from dyslexic CEOs to civil rights activists, Gladwell shows that limitations can produce not just resilience but transformation. Bjork’s work shows that our brains leverage desirable difficulties to learn. His work has deeply impacted my own, as Dr. Bjork has graciously shared his breakthrough insights with our advanced learning company as chair of our brain science advisory board since 2011. Changing How We Think About Learning Just before the Thanksgiving holiday break in 2025, I began to understand the full power of AI in training. It happened as I was testing our new conversational AI training agent that we use to train doctors and nurses on critical topics where mistakes can result in patients dying from medical error. Most people are not aware that the third leading cause of death in America, only behind heart attack and cancer, is death due to medical error. That’s one reason we take our work so seriously at my advanced learning company—we are all patients eventually. The seminal work that disclosed the extent of this critical medical error occurrence at a rate of 268 avoidable deaths per day was called To Err Is Human: Building a Safer Health System , published in 2000. 17 This report was deeply informed by the work of Dr. Brent James, a towering figure in the world of medical patient safety. Dr. James has chaired my company’s clinical innovation advisory board since 2019. It is important to understand that frontline healthcare workers are heroes who work in the most complex work environment on earth, in my opinion. Imagine a manufacturing line cranking out identical products one after another. Same materials, same process, rinse and repeat. Now imagine healthcare. The challenge is that you are combining the complexity of biology with comorbidity—patients have multiple issues at once, which impact treatment strategies and priorities—and adding distributed round-the-clock decision-making. Add to that, the science of medicine advances at an extraordinary and accelerating pace, making it very difficult to keep up. David Eddy, a key thought leader behind evidenced-based medicine, has said the “complexity of modern medicine exceeds the inherent limitations of the unaided human [expert] mind.” 18 The culmination of years of work was finally upon us as Thanksgiving approached, and I was testing the launch of our conversational AI training agent. I was being trained by my company’s AI training agent on one of the worst killers, sepsis, where an infection triggers a dangerous inflammatory response throughout the body.
